summary:
Ridgeline is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. For any of 33 sites, or coordinates you type in, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real terrain horizon, using NASA LOLA elevation data checked against JPL Horizons. Each scenario gets a verdict, the hours with both sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset. Up to four scenarios sit side by side.

Those numbers decide whether a lander near the south pole survives. The Sun never rises more than about 7° there, so a single ridge can cut off its power or its radio link to Earth, and a two-week delay can turn a Good site into a Poor one. IM-2 Athena landed on its side, couldn’t charge, and went silent within a day. Chandrayaan-3 got one lunar day of sunlight before the night ended it. Launch dates often slip, and each slip means rechecking every candidate site in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, tools built for specialists. Ridgeline does that recheck in seconds. With this app, we strongly believe that science and engineering teams can agree on a backup site quickly, saving time and cost. Students and the public can also learn how to use the website with our tutorial guide as well!
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Ridgeline answers one question for any landing site and date: will the lander have sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio, and for how long?

You pick a site from a list of 33 or type in coordinates, then set a landing date and time. Ridgeline works out where the Sun and Earth are in that site’s sky for the next 14 days, in 10-minute steps. It compares those positions with the real terrain horizon around the site. Each scenario card shows:

  • a Good, Marginal or Poor verdict
  • the hours when sunlight and an Earth view overlap
  • countdowns to sunset and Earthset
  • the longest stretch of darkness

You can put up to four scenarios side by side, for example the same site two weeks later, or a site a few kilometres away.

There are two halves under the hood:

  • Offline data pipeline (Python). It reads NASA’s SPICE files to get hourly Sun and Earth positions from 1969 to 2035. It then traces rays across NASA LOLA elevation maps to build a 360° horizon for every catalogue site, plus a grid of points within 190 km of the south pole.
  • Browser engine (TypeScript). It runs in a background thread and does the rest on your device, with no server involved. It accounts for the Sun’s and Earth’s full discs rather than single points, lunar eclipses, and the Sun sitting too close to Earth for radio.

On the screen you get:

  • a 3D view of the real terrain, with shadows
  • a 360° skyline view
  • a large map with the NASA permanent-shadow regions and a 20 km heatmap of nearby spots
  • a playable timeline
  • a year-long calendar that colours each day by how good a landing would be

What benefits does it have?

  • Speed. Comparing a date slip or a backup site takes seconds. Doing the same thing in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons means juggling three tools and reading raw numbers.
  • Shareable. The whole view lives in the URL, so a team can send each other exact scenarios. Cards also export to PNG and CSV.
  • Honest about uncertainty. Each headline number comes with a range: it is recomputed with the horizon nudged up and down and with the landing point moved around a 2 km landing ellipse.
  • Works anywhere. It runs on a phone, works offline after the first visit, and has no accounts, cookies or tracking.
  • Approachable. Every technical term has a tooltip, a 10-step guided tour walks through the app, and a short line contrasts the Moon with Earth.

What is the intended impact?

When a launch slips, mission teams should be able to see within minutes whether their landing site still works, and which nearby site or date does. That matters most near the south pole. The Sun there never rises more than about 7°, so one ridge can decide whether a lander gets power. IM-2 Athena landed on its side, couldn’t charge, and went silent within a day.

The second goal is teaching. A student can load the real landing moments of Chandrayaan-3, SLIM or IM-2 and see why each mission went the way it did.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript for the app and the calculation engine, Python for the data pipeline.
    • LOLA elevation maps of the south pole and the whole Moon
    • NAIF SPICE kernels (the DE440 ephemeris)
    • PGDA polar illumination and permanent-shadow maps
    • JPL Horizons as an independent accuracy check
    • links to LROC Quickmap and Moon Trek
  • Testing: Vitest (372 unit tests), pytest (81 pipeline tests) and Playwright (68 browser tests).
  • Hosting: code on GitHub, deployed on Vercel.
  • Hardware: one Windows laptop and a phone for testing. No special hardware.
  • AI help: AI has mainly used to perform large-scale data analysis and wrote most of the code. I directed and reviewed the work. The automated tests and the published validation against NASA and JPL data check correctness, so nothing relies on trusting the models.

How is your project creative?

  • It shows the horizon itself. Most tools give averages, such as “85% sunlit”. Ridgeline puts the actual skyline on screen and draws the Sun and Earth crossing it, so you can see which ridge blocks which hour.
  • It is built around the schedule-slip question. The main question is “is the new date better or worse, by how much, and why?”, not “show me the data”.
  • Real missions as test cases. You can replay Chandrayaan-3, SLIM and IM-2 and many other locations/landing sites at their real landing times.
  • Uncommon details. It models eclipses, the Sun interfering with Earth radio, a check on whether the lander can see Earth during the hour before touchdown, tip-over resilience, and Deep Space Network coverage. Most lighting tools skip these.
  • A scroll-driven landing page. It takes you from orbit down to the polar ridges before you reach the planner.

What factors did you consider?

  • Scientific accuracy first. The Sun positions match JPL Horizons to about 0.00001°, and Earth’s to about 0.0001°. The results are also checked against NASA’s lunar eclipse catalogue and the PGDA illumination maps. The About page shows every check, including the one that fails.
  • Saying what we don’t model. It has no thermal or battery model. Slope is shown in the 3D view but doesn’t affect the verdict, and the terrain detail stops at the grid spacing. The About page lists all of this, and visuals that are only illustrations are labelled as such.
  • No made-up data. Every site has a cited source. Planned missions with no published landing coordinates (Griffin-1, Blue Moon MK1, APEX at Schrödinger) are left out rather than guessed.
  • Accessibility. It has large touch targets of 44 px or more, full keyboard use, screen-reader labels, colour plus text for every state, and reduced motion for people who need it.
  • Phones and patchy connections. It is designed to be mobile-compatible as well, and does not require a large laptop to run.
  • Speed. Recomputing a scenario takes well under 150 ms, and the year calendar fills in under 1.5 s.
  • Privacy and cost. It is a static site with no backend, cookies or analytics, so it costs nothing to run.
